utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic to continue your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue immediately, but let me ask you first and foremost for a particular piece of information. Mr. Robinson, there are a great many documents here from General Stevanovic and Witness Jasovic. When do you think you would be able to look at these exhibits? You left that for later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We plan to do that very soon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just to complete the information, we're actually awaiting the translation of the submissions from the -- from your associates on that. I believe that has now come in, so we should be attending to that very soon. Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this binder that pertains to Racak, in tab 7 there is yet another report which I hope you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could a copy please be placed on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope you have it now.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This copy of yours in the Serbian language, is it legible? Mine is quite illegible.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think this is really legible either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read the date at least? Up on the top you can see "Urosevac," and you can see the date.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the date is the 16th of January, 1999, up here. Yes, the 16th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the heading?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it says up here the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, but I cannot see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the English translation we can see that it's MUP, Operational Centre of the MUP, the staff for Kosovo and Metohija. All of that is mentioned here, then Kacanik, Stimlje, Strpce, Djeneral Jankovic and Glogoscica. These are different police stations that were sent this document. That can be seen from the English translation. I can't read it in Serbian either. Now, look at the heading. The heading is rather legible.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The report on developments and events on the 15th of January, 1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say the 15th or the 16th? I think it says the 15th.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe it is the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If not, perhaps we can place it on the ELMO and we can have a look at it together because we can see the 16th typewritten up on the top of this survey.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 16th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whose signature's down at the end?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the shift of the duty service of the SUP of Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The head of the shift of the duty service of the SUP of Urosevac sent this survey of events for the 15th. And then point 1 states --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, point 1 states --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Something that has nothing to do with Racak. Item 2 is also -- and then on the second page there is a survey of what happened in Racak, also rather succinct. And the rest pertains to other events. Can you read this survey of events in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, just before you do that, could you also have in front of you tab 5 from that binder, and can you compare the part you're now being asked to read on tab 7 with tab 5 from the second paragraph and tell me if they are identical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't read this part from tab 7. You mean tab 7, the second paragraph. It says: "The 15th of January, 1999," if that's the passage you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Starting at 0300 hours, yes. That's the third -- it's on page 2 of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's headed "Other events and developments" in tab 7. The part you've just been directed to by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Other events and developments," on this page, this dispatch. "Other developments and events." The rest is rather illegible, what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it look to you identical to tab 5 from the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second paragraph, as far as I can see here from tab 7, well, I don't really find it very legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand Mr. Bonomy. He's asking you whether what it says in tab 7 -- whether what it says in tab 7 is identical to what it says in tab 5.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot read this paragraph from tab 7 and that's why I cannot give an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In all fairness, I can't read it either.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read this tab 7 at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this second page is illegible, the one I have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We will not torment ourselves with that any longer then. At any rate, in tab 7 from what can be seen is a survey of what happened on the 15th of January, sent by the head of the shift?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If the Court deputy could print out Prosecution Exhibit 211, then the witness can read it. It's tab 7. We can proceed at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I hope that the rest is legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at tab 9 now. In all fairness, you have nothing to look at in tab 9 because it was only given in the English language. It hasn't been translated. But this is a note from a meeting. The head of the Ministry of the Interior in Urosevac. It was held in Urosevac at the Secretariat of the Interior. I'm going to put some questions to you. Mr. Nice claimed that the army was involved in what happened in Racak. Here it says who was present at the meeting. Under (J) is Colonel Bogoljub Janicevic. It says Janicijevic, but that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a mistake. It's Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He's chief of the MUP secretariat. Then there's Brigadier General Maisonneuve, head of this centre from Prizren, then the deputy head of the centre from Pristina, and an interpreter. On page 2 -- or, rather, could we have it placed on the ELMO, because it's just in English. (G) is Gilbertson. (J) is Janicevic, and it says what they were talking about. We will start from line 10: "[In English] Who are the involved VJ? "Janicevic: Who says they were? "Gilbertson: OSCE saw it. US KDOM saw it. "Janicevic: VJ op checkpoint only."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The monitor should show the second -- next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have we got it at all on the monitor now? Let me just have a look. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Janicevic says the army of Yugoslavia is only at the checkpoint. Can you see that? Further on the question is: "Do police ever op --" operate, I assume -- "with the army of Yugoslavia? "I may not have that information. "Any prisoners taken?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's past time now for a question, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard, Mr. Jasovic, since you worked at the Urosevac secretariat, that in relation to Racak any military unit was engaged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days ago at this trial I said that I have never heard of this, and I never heard of members of the army of Yugoslavia being engaged in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then he asks him, M, I assume it's Maisonneuve -- if we look at the previous page, yes, it's Maisonneuve: "[In English] You were in charge of 100 policemen? "If it is of your concern, yes." [Interpretation] Now, the second one, Gilbertson, says: "[In English] We just left the VJ. They put all the blame on you. Were they with you or not? "Janicevic: We were not with the VJ." [Interpretation] Gilbertson asks: "Police were the only ones to do anything with this operation? "[In English] Janicevic: I guarantee you it was only police taking activities to stop or eliminate terrorists." [Interpretation] So the words uttered by Janicevic, is that consistent with what you knew?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the then chief, Bogoljub Janicevic, said is consistent with that. I know that the police took part in this operation. I didn't hear about the army participating.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to what you knew, was that a fully legitimate operation of the police or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as to this question, I assume --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Chamber might like to remind itself that when I asked about this tab, recognising it was in English, I confined myself to asking this witness whether he should think of any reason why Janicevic should deny the involvement of the VJ, and he said he didn't know the answer and most likely his former boss could answer. I'm really not sure these questions are doing anything except spending time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness knows nothing about this, as he said so, I think. Move on to another area, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice told us about the question that he asked, whether there was any reason, and I can tell you that the army was not involved there at all, and were it involved, I don't see why anybody would be concealing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The one thing that this accused cannot do is tell us anything, and I would invite the Court to restrain his attempts to use interventions and observations to do that which apparently he is not going to do, which is to take the solemn declaration and give evidence. And if he wants to ask the witness the questions that deal with -- that I dealt with which show the presence of the army, that's another matter, but simply to deal with something this witness can't deal with, which is what his boss said contrary to that evidence, is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another area, Mr. Milosevic. You're not to answer. Mr. Milosevic will ask you another question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His boss or, rather, the right person who is in position to answer, has given an answer, and I just read it out. It's in this record that I just read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just cover tab 15. This is the tab pertaining to which Mr. Nice claimed that some people had been executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read out the information. It is legible, completely clear. Since in the third line of the English translation it says "were executed." That's what it says here, "executed." Would you please read out the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I detect once again diminishing returns setting in. There comes a stage in your re-examination when you have obviously exhausted the topic. There is no obligation to go on, and certainly if you go on in this manner, it will be terminated. You have already spent a day and a half or two days re-examining the witness. If you have no further questions of a proper nature to put to the witness, then stop. Otherwise, the re-examination will be terminated. You're wasting time. We have been here for, what, about half an hour, and you have not asked even two questions that are worthwhile.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, in this information, the document entitled "Information," it is stated what are the grounds for suspicion concerning a terrorist group led by -- by Sadik Mujota, who apparently was liquidated in Racak on the 15th of January. Would you please tell us what is this group suspected of having committed? Do you have the first page, where it says that there are reasonable grounds to believe that this group led by Sadik Mujota committed a number of terrorists acts regulated by Article 125 of the criminal law of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as I can see here, we have 1, 2, 3, 4 bullets here, 5, 6, 7, 8. Does this information in fact detail what kind of a person this is and what has this person committed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on operative information, we learned that Sadik Mujota from the village of Malopoljce, Stimlje municipality, together with his terrorist group, committed a number of crimes of terrorist attacks in the territory of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The first bullet, can you read out the first word.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first word is "The killing of Mihajlovic Sinisa."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So the first word is the killing or the murder. And then further on it says the wounding as well. So the first one is murder. And then what about the second bullet, just read the first word.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murder of Jankovic Sasa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, murder as well. What about the third one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murder of Aluri Nazmija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So in this case an Albanian was killed. What about the fourth bullet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murder of Djordjevic Ranko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fifth one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murder of Resani Miftar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The sixth one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murder of Gasi Enver.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The seventh one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of January, the murder of Przic Svetislav, policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the last line, what does it say there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sadik Mujota, together with his terrorist group, participated in the setting on fire of the houses of members of Albanian minority in the village of Racak, Stimlje municipality, so that on the 11th -- 18th of November, 1998, at around 1730 hours they set on fire the house of Bitiqi Xhemajl in the village of Racak."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop a minute. Stop a minute. What is the purpose of this questioning, this line of questioning, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose is to establish that a document entitled "Information" was submitted on liquidation of a terrorist who had committed seven murders and that this person was killed in Racak. This is what the police learned, because they were unable to identify everyone at the time when these people died. Later on, they identified this person and established that this person had committed seven murders that police was aware, and of course many other crimes. So this Information discusses the acts committed by one of the persons killed in Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, is this a regular procedure, to compile a document entitled Information about such persons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is the regular procedure. This Information, document entitled "Information" tells us about the person who participated in terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And in tab 16, we have the Daily Bulletin, particularly quoted by Mr. Nice, where the head of the shift, sergeant first class, drafted a note on a conversation which we were able to see in the English text provided by the Verification Mission. Therefore, can we see here already on the second page that all of those persons mentioned by the Verification Mission are listed here as well? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Except it says "Dilbertson" instead of "Gilbertson," and then Maisonneuve and so on, as well as the chief of the Urosevac SUP. So is this actually the Serbian note about that meeting, that same meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally the chief of the Urosevac secretariat was fully authorised to conduct meetings at this level and have conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are you able to establish that this note, this document, is longer or shorter than the English version?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that this one is more complete, based on the description.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was supposed to be the role of the sergeant first class? Was his role simply that of a note-taker or note-writer or was he also participating in the conversation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most likely the chief of the secretariat took part in the conversation and then he conveyed to the head of the shift what to put in in the note describing the events of the day. I assume that such meetings are held at a higher level and then the chief of the secretariat authorises somebody to write up such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jasovic, that is not in dispute here; it's quite clear. I'm asking you, what was the role of the head of the shift? Was it just to write up the note or to do something else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his duty was to put in the document, describe all of the events which took place on the day when he was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Jasovic. Let us continue. Mr. Nice in the last few days particularly emphasised how unlikely it is for someone who -- of an advanced age, to be a member of the KLA. Would you please take the book that we looked at yesterday published by the Albanians, and let us just go over several examples of persons whom they included in the list of their heroes. We are not now dealing with Racak, we are dealing about the allegation that somebody of an advanced age must be a civilian. Would you please open up page 51, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, in what year was the fifth person from the top born?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamit Halit Lladrofci, born in 1920.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And died in 1998?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, I thought from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if we deduct 20 from 1998, what do we get?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 78, Mr. Jasovic, certainly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Let's take a look at page 55 now.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The last person on the list.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilaz Bali Hyseni.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Born in what year?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1915, killed in -- or died in 1998 in Kaqanoll.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was 83?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was 83. 98 minus 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this a document setting out KLA members or Albanians who -- UCK.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is their book, Mr. Robinson, the book that I received from the opposite side. This book contains the names of the fallen heroes, as they call them, members of the KLA who were killed, fallen heroes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Everybody in this book, in this document, is a KLA member, as distinct from just an Albanian. That's what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you were able to see the cover page of this book. You can have that translated. I don't have the translation. I have it in the Albanian language only. But you were able to see that there is the UCK written on the cover page, and we can also see the emblem. It states very clearly that this is the book on the fallen members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does this mean, Fenikset e Lirise, Fenikset e Lirise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Phoenix of Freedom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then please look at page 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, 66. The third person from the top, born in 1926. So he was 74, 72, killed in 1998.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us not continue with this, but Mr. Jasovic, based on your experience, were you familiar with any cases where some very old people or some very young persons, in fact minors, were members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. The KLA was not a legal institution that applied the same rules as the army, because the army, for example, takes people 18 and up only. In this case, anybody who was fit, who was able, could join the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question. Upward limit. Upward age. What is the oldest that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are no rules. I don't know who the oldest was, oldest KLA member. I can't remember. But as for the KLA generally, I said that only able people were -- they might be somebody who is 70 but quite capable and able, if I can put it that way. So there are no strict rules according to which a person joins the KLA, say, from the ages of 15 to 55, or any such specifications. Anybody who was able or capable could join.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to give a name of a very young person or a very old person that you were aware of as a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The KLA members -- well, let me take the example of Afrim Musliu from the Belinc village. They were young then, very young guys. Afrim and his brother, they were young men. I can't remember. Well, they were about -- under the age of 20 certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Now, we saw in this book a person who was 83 years old. Mr. Jasovic, you received, as it says here, a partial translation of a statement by a protected witness who is to be found in tab 9 of Mr. Nice's documents. I'm going to quote just one point from that partial translation, because the others were ones that Mr. Nice quoted to you. It is point 47, in fact, of tab 9. But since it wasn't translated very precisely, I'm going to read it from the English, point 47, because in the translation it says, "Jasovic in 1997 and 1998," whereas in paragraph 47, it says: "In 1997/8/9." So one year has been left out in the translation. He "concentrated on members of the KLA, which he referred to as terrorists, whom he called terrorists, in the area around Stimlje, Urosevac, and the villages of those two municipalities." So here it says that you were concentrating on that. And was that your job precisely as a crime inspector, to learn as much as you could about members of the KLA during those years?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 1998, for instance, with the appearance of the KLA staffs and headquarters that were set up. Within the frameworks of my line of work, I worked together with my colleague, and one of my assignments was to connect all information linked and related to the KLA. And as I said earlier on, information about their activities, movements, how many of them there were, what weapons they had. So our operative work was focused on throwing light on them and finding the perpetrators of possible terrorist acts that had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we're moving on from any reference or further reference to the book "Fallen Heroes," the Chamber will recall the limited questions I felt able to ask of this witness in relation to it, because of course he knew nothing of its compilation. And the Chamber will also recall that in the questions I asked I in no sense accepted that all those described there were in any sense active members of the KLA. I explained through questions to the witness that materials can be found, indeed I think about tabs -- tabs 8 and 9, I think -- or no, not 8 and 9. Materials can be found showing the problems there were with compilation of this book and the reasons why people's names might be in it, but in light of Your Honours' questions, it is not put in on the basis that the Prosecution accepts -- it's not put in at all, but it's -- if it is to go in as an exhibit, it's not accepted by the Prosecution that the people named there are automatically members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is it then?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was a document that it was thought appropriate because of course it provides some significant material to indicate that people may be members of the KLA, but there are also other reasons for names appearing there, at least on the material coming for us; pension and matters of that sort, people wanting their names there because they want to be registered as heroes, whatever their contribution. And so it would be incorrect to rely on the document as in any sense an admission by the Prosecution that somebody in that book is a member of the KLA. Notwithstanding that, I've drawn to your attention the fact that there is a coincidence between those listed there, for example, and those identified by Shukri Buja, but then there is a non-coincidence between those identified as civilians and three of the names found in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You won't be seeking to have this exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm content to have it exhibited in due course, but we'll have to consider exhibits much more generally. I don't object to its being exhibited, we made it available to the accused in order to help him, but by doing that we're not saying that the document is in some way authoritative of who was or was not a member of the KLA at the time of their death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Has the introductory narrative been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It hadn't. I don't think it's been translated into English [microphone not activated]... There are those in Court who can help you, including the witness, with what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember a part of Mr. Shukri Buja's evidence where he said that not all the KLA members were engaged in combat operations. Some of them were only involved in administrative matters or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that's indeed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please Mr. Nice. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies. That is indeed correct, but in a recent statement dealing with this book, and with other matters which you can find at tab 7 and there's another at tab 8 that deals with it, you can find his further qualification for categorisation of people in this book. If necessary and -- this evidence can be called at a later stage in the trial if it becomes sufficiently critical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's a fairly long introduction. Perhaps that would throw some light --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- on the status of those whose names are included.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that can always be translated, and we can possibly look at it on the overhead projector now through this witness. I should explain again, and I think I explained earlier, there are some other books which we made available which are individual biographies of some of those who are named in the general index, biographies with photographs. We've gone through those in particular to see if we can find any of the three people described in Schedule A as civilians having a detailed biography that would show how they died at Racak, because obviously that would be potentially interesting and favourable to the accused. They don't show, as far as we've been able to discover in those subsequent biographies, and we've been unable to unearth anything favourable to the accused in those subsequent biographies where more detail is provided, but all the material's available to him for him to deal with as he wishes, subject to the limitations on the material as Shukri Buja describes it. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this the same material we dealt with during the -- Mr. Stevanovic's evidence? I remember we once -- we saw similar material which was disclosed under the regime of 68 to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it -- we may have dealt with it with Mr. Stevanovic, and certainly I think it had been disclosed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I remember is Phoenix of Freedom, or something like that. We saw the similar --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I'll check that. Reminding that Court that although it was nominally provided under Rule 68 that was out of an excess of concern for the accused not necessarily knowing that something was available in open sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The introduction should be translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the Court so decides, we'll get it done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we ask that it be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson -- yes, it's on. I can -- Mr. Nice mentioned the testimony of Shukri Buja. I don't have time to deal with his testimony now, however, you can glance through his statement and you'll be able to see that they endeavoured to introduce names restrictively and not on an extensive basis; that is to say, not to put somebody on the list that just happened to die somehow but whom according to their criteria deserved and merited being on the pages of that book of fallen heroes. So that that gives me quite enough reason to believe that these are exclusively fallen KLA fighters, those who fell in battle. And anyway, we can establish that later on. But it's quite clear why, and I'm very surprised to see why Mr. Nice, who provided me with this book, now suddenly has some reservations to make. The only thing that can be said is that it is probably not complete and comprehensive. I'm sure there are more names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, let's try and save as much time as possible now. You were asked by Mr. Nice whether you knew anything about the visit of General Djordjevic to the SUP of Urosevac. Now, please, do you remember what General Djordjevic was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Djordjevic was there in the capacity of deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia, I believe. I think at the time he was chief of the sector for public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. As chief of public security, was General Djordjevic the immediate superior to the chiefs of the Secretariats of the Interior in the whole of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course that's true, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, then, is there anything unusual in the fact that the immediate superior should tour the Secretariats of the Interior, should visit the Secretariats of the Interior in the field, or would it be unusual if he were not to visit them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be unusual if he did not visit them and tour them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... referred you to his superiors. So this is, although expressed in an alternative format so as not to be strictly speaking leading, is effectively a leading question on a topic that the witness has said in earlier testimony he can't help with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he can ask the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I didn't know whether he visited the secretariat in Urosevac that particular day, the day you specified. I don't know that. That's what I said I didn't know. But, yes, it is customary and usual that he can come any time to tour the Secretariat of the Interior, pay them a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I have one more tab of Mr. Nice's to get through, and he focused on it especially. And that is tab -- the last tab, in fact, in this binder of his. It is 2.23. That is the number which it goes by, and it refers to a statement by Adil Zymberi, if I'm reading it correctly, if I'm reading his name correctly. They interviewed him and questioned him with respect to all the statements he provided, and you have here as a supplement your own information at the end. If you could take a look at that, Mr. Jasovic, the report at the end.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found the report or information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is dated the 20th of January, 1999. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. It says report/6-99 of the 20th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, Mr. Jasovic, since this is rather a lengthy report, and in the statement of Mr. Zymberi, which as we can see was taken on the 29th of May, 2005, can you read when the statement was taken? Do you see that date, the 29th of May, 2005? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zymberi Fadil. The date is the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you took the statement on the 20th of January, 1999, did you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this now, please, Mr. Jasovic: Can you remember the circumstances under which you took the statement, which as I can see is a very detailed one, very extensive, comprehensive, contains many facts. And Mr. Nice's witnesses here said that that was the job you were engaged in, collecting information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find Fadil Zymberi's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's at the end. Try and find it, please. Towards the end.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to have my statement except the statement which he gave to the investigators or, rather, this seems to be my statement in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you must have a photocopy of the version in Serbian. I'm sure you do somewhere.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have this information dated the 20th of January, 1999. As for Fadil Zymberi's statement, I haven't got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that Fadil Zymberi's statement, the one that you had from the 20th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's tab 2.23. And this is a particular piece of information containing information about the whereabouts of the KLA. This information was proffered by the informer and a male nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You saw that Fadil Zymberi is challenging a series of information contained --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- in this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- incorrect summary and the witness is indeed revealing the history of this document. The witness gave two different accounts for the source of this document. As I think I heard one of the Bench say, there is no statement from Zymberi, so it is not correct for the accused to summarise the position as a statement of Zymberi. This document, whatever else it may be in light of the two answers in the course of his evidence given, or explanations given by this witness, is not an apparent statement of anybody, and it doesn't divide up, if there were two sources of information, who provided what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for the correction, Mr. Nice. It's headed a report, or Information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm afraid that it's a misunderstanding. I am not saying that this Information - because that is actually the heading of this document, it is Information, not Report - I'm speaking of Zymberi's statement contained in tab 2.23 that you have here in English. Zymberi Fadil gave his statement on the 29th of May, 2005. So I asked the witness when this person gave the statement. In his statement, he brings into question what is contained in this information. So I wish to confront his claims in the Information with the knowledge of the witness contained in the statement and also what he included in this piece of information. Mr. Nice also gave a summary of statement here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the statement -- I think we have it now. The statement is the first document in 2.23. The second document, yes. The first is a summary. What is the specific question now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness does not have Zymberi's statement and this summary of statement of Zymberi, because it's in English and that has not been translated for him, and it is actually different from what he states in his Information, I think it would be a good thing for him to compare Zymberi's summary of statement to the positions contained in his Information and to say who it is that is telling the truth or, rather, that he testify to what the truth actually is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The male nurse, there's probably a misunderstanding here because even now I cannot remember the name and surname of the male nurse. I've simply forgotten his name and surname. Tab 2.23 relates to two sources. Two persons gave me information; the informer and the male nurse. Even now I cannot remember the name of the male nurse because I saw him only two or three times. I cannot say whether his name is Fadil Zymberi and whether he's the person who gave the Prosecution a statement. He said that he's a male nurse, probably he is that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not for you to establish what is probable or likely, Mr. Jasovic. Your information is very extensive, and it contains a great deal of information, and he confronted that with Fadil Zymberi's statement, who claims that did he not say some of the things that are contained in your Information. Where in this Information of yours do you claim that you learned this from Fadil Zymberi?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person lives in the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a moment. In your Information, is it stated anywhere that you got this information from Fadil Zymberi? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not written there. As I've already said, I can compile an Information without giving the names of the persons who provided me with information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, Mr. Nice claims that you got this information from Fadil Zymberi, who denies that. So I'm asking you, did you get the information from Zymberi or did you get it from some other people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it from a male nurse. Even now I cannot remember whether his name is Fadil Zymberi. That is why we have this misunderstanding, because I cannot recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry to interrupt, but with this line of approach to re-examination, it's necessary to nip things in the bud. On the 27th of April of this year, this witness gave the following unqualified explanation for tab 2.23: He said the information was provided by a nurse from the village of Racak whose name he couldn't recall, but he could state that the male nurse was married to a woman from the village of Petrastica, Stimlje municipality, that his father-in-law I think is called Dugolli, killed on the 28th of November of 1997. Those coordinates were pursued by the investigator Ms. Murtagh. This person was the unique identified person who resulted from the information provided by this witness on the 27th of April. Association of the material with another person came at other times, but on this occasion he was quite specific. And the Court will have in mind --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will have in mind, if it's looking at the witness -- or proposed witness statement in tab 2.23, that the last paragraph of the witness statement sets out his account of his own history, which matches that given for the person concerned by this witness on the 27th of April of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I took note of your comment, Mr. Nice, about this type of re-examination, because I'm getting very concerned about the manner in which the re-examination is conducted. I have spent 37 years in adversarial proceedings, and I have never witnessed re-examination of this length, no matter how long the cross-examination is. Mr. Kay, maybe you can tell me if you have seen re-examination last one day or two days. I've never seen it, no matter how long the cross-examination is. Re-examination is simply for the purpose of rehabilitating your witness, dealing with important points that arise out of cross-examination. And I have to consult my colleagues about this as to whether we are discharging our duties properly. The re-examination should not last two days. That's an abuse of the entire process. The re-examination should be conducted in the same way it would be conducted in Jamaica or in Scotland or in England or in Canada, in countries which have adversarial proceedings. Re-examination is not to last a day or two days. It's abusive, and I will consult with my colleagues in the break as to how to constrain this kind of re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would say even shorter in civil law countries as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. One of the problems is that -- and it's necessary in the terms of the constraints we face. Mr. Nice, in his cross-examination, was able in an almost seamless way to bring Your Honours in by way of comment, often not solely directed to the witness, and tie up issues of argument and presentation that was in his interest that he wanted to make time and time again. I didn't do anything about that, but it was obvious to me that there was a form of presentation that was in the form of speech as well as questioning. One understands the limits that we have in terms of time, and sometimes a message has to be got over in a way that requires a degree of latitude, and it may be that some habits that have been brought into the questioning of witnesses are necessarily copied and reflected by the Defence in the way sometimes that Mr. Milosevic has to present his points which he feels need to be tied up so that Your Honours understand it, and that seems to have been a practice that has been developing in the questioning of witnesses. That's all I have to say about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Milosevic, how much longer do you plan to spend?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope I finish before the end of this session. If Mr. Nice were not interrupting me all the time, I would have finished by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I take that -- I doubt that, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot ask the witness now to read the text in English, but I would like to draw your attention to the following: In relation to this Information that was provided by the witness, dated the 20th of January, 1999, and that somebody marked according to paragraphs, please look at the summary. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine paragraphs from the bottom -- I haven't even gone on to the other page, and then the other page one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine -- 18, 18 paragraphs contain the same phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, listen to this, Mr. Jasovic. Listen to the phrase: "[In English] He stated he is not the origin of the information." [Interpretation] So in 18 paragraphs contained in this Information, or more, I referred only to 18, but, no, there are more. Again towards the end there are more. Not the origin, not the origin, and so on. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber has difficulty locating the paragraph. Could you do that again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Take the first document from 2.23. Fadil Zymberi, OTP Summary of Statement. And then -- and then look at the bullets on that page. Nine bullets, counting from the bottom. In all of those nine paragraphs it says that he is not the source of information. And on the second page this is referred to in ten or 12 further bullets, that he is not the origin of the information in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you, Mr. Jasovic, if he claims that he is not the origin of information for at least half of this Information that you provided here, could you explain to me whether you simply invented what is contained in this Information or did you receive information from a trustworthy source, a source that is reliable enough for you to include this in an official Information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact is and the truth is that this information that I compiled I got from the male nurse and from the informer. As I said last time, this information came from two sources, that is to say two persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would particularly like to draw your attention to the following, that he says concerning paragraph 30 -- I'm going to read it in English so that I won't make a mistake: "[In English] In paragraph 30 he states that contrary to that stated in tab 2.23, he does not know if the persons mentioned therein were KLA members." [Interpretation] Now, that is on page 3 of your statement. It is marked as paragraph 30. It says: "In addition to the aforementioned members of the so-called KLA, the following were also in the village of Racak," and then there is a long paragraph containing at least 30 names. Did you invent that, Mr. Jasovic, or did you receive this information from your informer or any other source? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not invent this information, neither I nor my colleague Momcilo Sparavalo. We received this information from a male nurse and from our informer. For me this information is trustworthy and truthful, because these persons appear in other documents as well as members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not going to deal with this any longer. I just wanted to indicate the quality of the evidence that Mr. Nice compiled in 2005.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how that works in that system of yours that you keep referring to all the time, Mr. Robinson, but if somebody is not a source of information, then how can that person deny information that is contained in documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our instructions, we can compile Official Notes or this kind of information without referring to the name of the source, of the person that we talked to without revealing the details of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about what Mr. Nice said. He even went as for as to say that General Djordjevic exerted pressure for you to provide this kind of information. Please, is there a grain of truth in what Mr. Nice is claiming?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this at all, that General Djordjevic could exert pressure on me or anyone else for us to invent information, to make it up. Not only General Djordjevic, anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice also took as an example your tab 1.16, where one of the statements -- never mind, but 1.16 is your tab. And somebody wrote in hand on the top of the page "For Colonel General V. Djordjevic." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that most probably the head of the organ of the secretariat in Urosevac forwarded this note or information to General Djordjevic, which is only natural, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Jasovic, have I understood you correctly? Can I infer that if the head of the organ deems a particular piece of information of particular interest he sends it to his superior, and that is General Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to General Djordjevic, it's also the head of the MUP -- the staff of the MUP for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Jasovic, in these statements and in what Mr. Nice said, you were accused of having beaten people. Then you were presented with some kind of text of a certain Council for the Protection of Freedoms and so on. Over all those years, some NGO, some Council for the Protection of Freedom, some individual who was allegedly mistreated in the police, did anybody ever file a complaint against you or other members of the Ministry of the Interior in the secretariat in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No complaint was certainly filed against me. As for others, I cannot say. But I can say one thing here, that from the very beginning of my work, the then-head of secretariat Jusuf Karakushi commended me and gave me citations, and others after him, and that can be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 16, in a statement given by one of Mr. Nice's witnesses, this witness claims that you threatened him, that you threatened to chop his head off, and as it turned out later, you let him go. Is there a shred of truth in what Mr. Nice put to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no truth whatsoever, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said that somebody was beaten in February of 1999. In February of 1999, was there the European Mission of observers present as well as the OSCE Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we know that the Kosovo Verification Mission arrived in the fall of 1998, and I think that they left in February of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: March of 1999, Mr. Jasovic, not in February.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So if nobody complained to our organs, as Mr. Nice claims, did they have occasion to complain to the organs of the Verification Mission or the EU Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly they had occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that, Mr. Nice [as interpreted]: Do you know of anybody complaining to the members of the Verification Mission or the EU Observer Mission?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, you saw all of these documents, the facts; you were there in the Urosevac SUP. Do you remember, when it comes to weapons, weapons such as heavy machine-guns, plain machine-guns, hand grenades, so on, how much of that was found in the village of Racak? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said last time, quite a large quantity was found in the village of Racak when the on-site investigation was conducted. All of that weaponry was brought in into the hall of the Urosevac SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that clear that that weaponry was used to conduct combat?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Totally inadmissible leading question and I should remind the Court that this witness, so he told us, was never present in Racak himself, although I had material to suggest that he was. But no doubt he can always make that clear if it's going to be of any value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's -- that was leading --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not present in Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the weaponry because this was confiscated by your secretariat. Mr. Nice claims that the members of the Mother Teresa Association were killed in Racak. In your police experience did you ever hear of members of the Mother Teresa Association firing from heavy machine-guns, throwing hand grenades, and possessing all of that weaponry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN JASOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of the members of the Mother Teresa Organisation or Association firing or possessing all of that weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jasovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have further questions, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But there existed -- Mr. Jasovic, there existed an association which is called Mother Teresa Association there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about that association, the Mother Teresa Association, but I don't know whether it actually existed in Racak. I know that there was that association in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jasovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good-bye, Mr. President. Thank you to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, would there be other documents that you would wish to have exhibited other than what you have specifically referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The -- out of our binders, out of our two binders does Your Honour mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got three binders now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you've also tendered other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need to identify what it is you're seeking to --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Can I make our position clear? I'm going to seek to exclude all the Jasovic materials as unreliable and falling below a level that should be admitted. If that application succeeds, then little or none of the material that I've been relying on would be material I'd want admitted. Some of it might be valuable independently of the cross-examination of the witness, but if there's any question of the materials of Jasovic being admitted as evidence in this trial, then I would seek to have nearly all our materials admitted. I realise the Chamber may be against me in principle on, for example, the statements taken in accordance with its earlier rulings but I'll nevertheless make that application, but the other materials I think might be of value but the one would depend, in a sense, on the other. It had occurred to me that so far as the admission of the Jasovic materials are concerned, written submissions might be helpful but I'm entirely in the Court's hands. And if there were to be written submissions, could I respectfully invite the Court to consider as a -- on this particular occasion, inviting or demanding written submissions with the possibility for short, focused oral submissions when they've all been presented. Because I think it's quite an important issue and it might benefit from five or ten minutes from all the parties when the written submissions are in, rather than, for example, written submission and then replies and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we want to have a -- identify a reasonable time for the parties within which to make their submissions. Can I hear from you on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I would obviously hope to have staff to turn to it if -- pretty well immediately, but seven days might be optimistic and I prefer two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that's too much really. Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We should really be dealing with this by oral argument so that we can move on. The trouble is when we're -- the case moves on, we're going back to deal with these arguments that take two or three days to draft and put everything together in a proper way. Meanwhile, one's dealing with the new witnesses and other issues, and it's very difficult for the case to keep its forward-going momentum, and we are ready for our oral argument on the issues, which are very current, very pertinent. We've heard the evidence, we know what the conflict is about in the courtroom, and if both sides were given ten minutes to deal with oral argument on the admissibility, that might assist the Trial Chamber more than having more filings and more delay. That's my submission on the matter. As far as the compendium of Racak materials goes, the single volume, I think there's only one document that didn't come through in the form of a previous exhibit that was referred to in evidence. That seems to me a helpful matter, to have all the documents in one place, because it was becoming very difficult to trace many of the Racak documents in dealing with Racak issues, and that might be a useful aid to the Trial Chamber. They may have made their own compendiums already, we were putting that together, but this seems to me to be a useful collection, if we could get that out of the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I think that this would not fit in any system, what Mr. Nice is doing. You know very well he was the one who proposed to have this witness give evidence when I didn't even know that this witness existed. I accepted that, the witness came to testify, and brought with him original material created at the time of the events, contemporaneously. You gave Mr. Nice one month to prepare for cross-examination, and then Mr. Nice brought in some statements taken in May of 2005 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just comment on the particular issue at hand, written statements -- written submissions on the exhibits. If so, how long; or just oral arguments?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I am categorically opposed to written arguments, written submissions. I think that it is a normal procedure to have exhibits admitted during the testimony of the witness, to have them admitted or to deny their admission. I think this is normal procedure. And let me tell you right away I'm not going to write any written submissions on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In my system, yes, Mr. Milosevic. I understand that in some civil countries the admission is done at the end of the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, in your system you can do as you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what we are to decide is what is the best course of action in the particular circumstances of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is the Chamber's ruling on this matter: If the Prosecution wishes to put in written submissions on the question of exhibits, it may do so, but it must do so by Monday of next week, and then on Wednesday of next week we'll have -- we'll hear oral arguments on the questions. If Mr. Kay wishes to put in a response, then you may do so, but there's no obligation to do that. We'll have a brief oral hearing on Wednesday of next week for arguments on the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about all of these documents and exhibits which were used during the testimony of General Stevanovic? There are some 17 binders of documents, and I'm afraid that we will have too great a distance from his testimony. And this pause that we're making between the testimony and the admittance of documents really leaves a very open possibility for misunderstanding and problems later on. Mr. Nice just said that there is a binder about Racak. Yes, that's right. That's within Mr. Nice's documents. And within General Stevanovic's documents there are two Racak binders, and so on and so on. There is a great number of documents used during the testimony here that you said would be considered later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's a good point. We don't want too much time to pass between the witness's evidence and the admission of exhibits relating to that evidence. We have that in mind. What has held up our consideration of Mr. Stevanovic's exhibits was the translation of the submissions from your associates. We expect to deal with that sometime next week. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next witness is General Bozidar Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And with what matters will he be dealing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Delic will be testifying about all the activities of the army of Yugoslavia under his command. And for your information, he commanded very important units of about 14.000 men who controlled some 140 kilometres of the state border and several towns in-depth, as well as many, many villages which comprise the area of those towns and relates to all the events that are vital in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Bear in mind, of course, the requirement that the evidence be relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am bearing in mind the fact, Mr. Robinson, that Mr. Nice during many of his examinations and assertions, he spoke about a pattern of behaviour on the part of the army of Yugoslavia, some kind of pattern on the part of the army and the police of Serbia. But now I'm just going to speak about the army of Yugoslavia. And with reference to that, it's very important to see what that pattern of behaviour looked like and how the army of Yugoslavia behaved, what the army of Yugoslavia did throughout that period of time in order to be able to see that in fact everything that Mr. Nice is implying when he uses the word "pattern" in connection with the army activities is just not true or correct, and you will have a chance to see what the army did over a continuous period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the evidence of this pattern may not necessarily relate to particular incidents in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They will relate to specific assertions, incidents, et cetera, and the overall behaviour and conduct of the army and units under his command throughout the material time that he's testifying about, the time relevant for what Mr. Nice is claiming, because you can't hide behind general phrases any more as to what somebody did or didn't do if there are specific data, concrete facts about the conduct of the Yugoslav army and how it acted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And just the last question: His evidence will be confined to this issue of pattern?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only to that but to concrete events and his knowledge of them, of the overall situation in Kosovo and Metohija or, rather, the knowledge that a commander of such a large body of men can have or has. So therefore, it will relate to all the events that are tied in to Mr. Nice's claims and allegations, and of course his witnesses too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I wonder if you can assist me. It may be impossible, but I was trying to identify any evidence so far of the involvement of the 549th Motorised Brigade, which appears to be a relevant army brigade, in any specific event charged in the indictment. Are you able to tell me if there is any such evidence? So far I'm unable to find any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm unable to do that just off the top of my head because the indictment refers to "Serb forces," as the Bench will know. It would have to be something that will have to be looked at. It's not something we've been picking out as a point when going through the evidence, so I can't take that any further, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I found it referred to in events that are not in the indictment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and serious events at that, but none that appear to actually be in the indictment. But however, if later you can assist, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness comes in, this not being in any sense his responsibility, documents, the position is that we've now got an index of 629 A documents, so it's obviously in excess of that number, which is more in number even than Stevanovic produced. So far as we've been able to judge, none of them was listed on the 65 ter listing of exhibits, and we've made inquiries to see if it's said that any of them were listed 65 ter, and it appears probably not. The material was first provided in B/C/S on the 14th of June, and Ms. Dicklich had to arrange for all of that material to be copied and scanned in order to process it because of the format in which it came in. Since then, translations have been coming in daily so that it's now 269 with English translations and 310 without. It would, of course, be possible for me to mount an argument saying that all of this written material should be excluded as in defiance of or in breach of your earlier rulings, and particularly attractive as a possibility to do that, given the time that the accused's evidence is taking and the problems that we've articulated in writing that will be forthcoming with the 150-day time limit generally. However, I recognise that within the documents produced there are some documents that I would want to rely on, insofar as I've been able to have the advantage of an assessment of them so far, there will be some documents that I would want to rely on in cross-examination. But in dealing with this witness, I would ask the Chamber to recognise the difficulties that we are placed under and difficulties that may become apparent with particular documents if they're not in translation at the time the witness comes to deal with them. We have done, as with all other witnesses, everything we can to assist in the presentation of the material, but there are limits to how far we can or should go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what is the explanation? What is the explanation for these documents which you intend to exhibit not being on the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, my explanation is this: First of all, the fact that I had an exceedingly short period of time to supply the documents on the first list; and the second explanation is that it is not unusual and that Mr. Nice would send in many documents post festum, later on during the course of his examination. Now, as far as the assertion that he made that he received it on the 14th of June, I cannot be of assistance to you there except to tell you that all the documents or, rather, all the exhibits which go with General Delic's testimony were sent in on 20th of April, which means two months ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But is the position that not even one of your proposed exhibits was on the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm that because I wasn't in a position to compare all those facts and information. But I did draw your attention to the fact that many archives were inaccessible to me and that my associates only managed, after a long period of time, to come by certain documents which are relevant for the Court here, to be presented here. So when they came by the documents, they became accessible, and without exception all of them were sent in on the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to add something, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wish to add is this: Many of the documents are documents which Mr. Nice's office does have because General Delic sent them in as an expert in the Haradinaj case. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can see you're familiar with all the standard arguments, Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice, can you comment on this? Mr. Milosevic says that the documents were sent on the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely I can comment on that, and it's one of the three points I wanted to make. The documents may have been provided to Registry, none of them was provided to us until last week; and indeed a second point is that when collections like this are provided by the accused, he retains a control over their provision to us until the last minute so that we aren't necessarily getting the complete collections, we're only getting what he's finally approved to pass. Now, there may be forensic reasons for that happening in light of one or two documents that, as it were, slipped through in the Stevanovic materials. We can understand from an entirely forensic point of view why he might want to do that, but the fact of the matter is the materials were here in April. If they'd been provided to us in April, we could have at least started working on them because of course we do have B/C/S readers, and we can start the process of analysing them even though only with a limited number of our team members. So that's the answer to that point. The last point I wanted to make is this: Mr. Saxon, who has been getting to grips with the documents at this stage rather more in earnest than I have, has identified several, or it may be many, stamped with a stamp that indicates they were provided by the VJ, presumably to this accused, from their archives in October 2002. So getting on for three years ago. Those are the points I wanted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That partially puts paid to your contention, Mr. Milosevic, that many of these documents were not accessible to you.
