Well, the Chamber's ruling is as follows: Mr. Milosevic, you must make a written application by tomorrow for the addition of all of these documents that you intend to exhibit, a written application for them to be added to the exhibit list with an explanation as to why they should be added.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, with respect to what Mr. Nice said a moment ago about tactics, let me tell you straight away I have no tactics to keep back any documents. From the moment the documents are handed over to the Registrar, every document is accessible to Mr. Nice's office, or can be accessible. So I never made any requests to hold back any documents and not to hand documents over to his office. The question is the speed at which this is done, whether this is done only once the documents have been translated or whether they supply them with untranslated documents, I don't know. That is out of my hands. But let me repeat here and now, and this holds true for everything, that everything that was handed over to the Registrar can be provided to Mr. Nice's office straight away. I have no need to keep anything back or make any delays in handing over the material. Now, as far as your request is concerned that I should make a written application for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not a request. It's an order. It's an order of the Chamber. If you intend to rely on these documents, you must apply in writing to have them added to the exhibit list. You're in flagrant violation of the Rules, and not for the first time. In the meantime, we'll proceed hearing the evidence, but by tomorrow you must have a written application for the addition of all of these documents to the exhibit list, with an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I understood it that by handing over the documents and their lists this was done, that is to say is that what you're asking now was fulfilled by handing over the documents linked to the testimony of this next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will not comment on that. You're seeking to make a mockery of the proceedings, Mr. Milosevic. Call the witness. We'll deal with the witness today, but as from tomorrow any document on which you intend to rely must be included in a written application to have the documents admitted, with an explanation. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, one matter just to assist the Court entirely differently, on the issue of the 549th Motorised Brigade: Witness K41 gave evidence at length in September of 2002, 6th of September 2002, on the operations of the brigade in the Prizren-Orahovac-Suva Reka area, used by the Prosecution in relation to paragraph 54 of the indictment, Article 7(1), criminal responsibility, and paragraphs 55. I'm talking to you as I'm doing a search. Paragraph 56. The issue of widespread and systematic would obviously arise. Paragraph 66, killing site overview. He's in the Prosecution fillbox document. As it's within Orahovac-Suva Reka area, it may be one of those units that the Prosecution are relying on under the general title of "Serb forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I've been trying to do is make the link between the specific reference to that force or that brigade in the evidence and any of the particular crime sites that are labelled, but I can't make the link. I see the point you're making.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I do have the evidence of K41.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do remember Maisonneuve referred to this brigade and the particular general and spoke of the qualities of the general. This isn't because of an excessively prodigious memory but merely the fact that it was a topic I was looking at fairly recently in relation to other research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And again I have -- you have identified the two principal witnesses that I seem to have identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Higgins has found Maisonneuve on 29th of May, 2002, when he gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just while that's happening and in light of the earlier discussion, we will now seek provision of documents relating to the forthcoming witness Bulatovic, which are even more voluminous in number, and we'll try and get them as soon as they are possible in order that we can process them as early as possible. In response to Your Honour's other inquiry, Bela Crkva is also within the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, would you please tell us where you were born and introduce yourself generally, in the briefest terms, the outlines.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, my name is Bozidar Delic, major general of the army of Serbia and Montenegro. I was born on the 20th of February, 1956, in the vicinity of Djakovica in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us briefly what education you've had and your professional experience.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: In addition to the military academy, which I graduated from in 1987, I went to the command staff school as well of the army of Yugoslavia and the national defence school of the army of Yugoslavia. That means that with regard to training and education, I'm on a par with a doctor of science, Ph.D., strategy, operations and tactics. I was also a lecturer at the tactics department of the military academy, and my professional title is docent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, what were you during the war in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: During the war in Kosovo, I was commander of the 549th Motorised Brigade, which was located in the garrisons of Prizren and one battalion was detached and located in the Djakovica garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you have a map beside you. Would you please show us and indicate your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: On this map we can see my zone of responsibility. Part of it cannot be seen here but my area of responsibility started from the Morina border post on the state border between --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... unless the audiovisual booth films it for me, if the board is at that angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let that be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My area of responsibility on the state border between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Albania, Morina, the border post of Morina. Then along the state border to the border between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the Republic of Albania, and the Republic of Macedonia. Then the state border with the Republic of Macedonia and -- that is to say between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Macedonia all the way up to the Peskovi mountain top on Mount Sara. From Peskovi on Mount Sara, the pass of Prevolac, Mount Osman, then Sar-Planina, Bukova Glava, then east of Suva Reka, Precevsko Brdo, then the pass of Dulje, Luznica, and at the north-east to Klecka, about one kilometre. Then east of Malisevo about two kilometres, then along the valley -- along the valley of the river to Beli Drim. Then the valley of Decanska Bistrica, here to Ljumbarde, the village of Ljumbarde, and then Lake Radonjic, Erecka Suka, and back to the Morina border post on the state border between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Albania. What I showed now is peacetime area of responsibility. In the war there was wartime area of responsibility which included a considerably smaller territory than what I showed just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, which towns and villages -- I'm actually referring to big towns and -- that belonged to your zone of responsibility in war and peace?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: In addition to Prizren, where the command of my brigade was, there was also Dragas, Suva Reka, Orahovac, Djakovica. But in Djakovica there was another brigade too. So as far as control over Djakovica, from 1997 onwards I did not have Djakovica under my control, although it was within my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, throughout 1998 and until mid-June 1999, were you in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout 1998 and 1999, I was in Kosovo and Metohija with one exception, about two months when I would spend weekends with my family in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say two months, how are we supposed to understand that, that once in every two months you would sometimes go to visit your family?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Say every two months I'd spend two or three days with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, throughout that time that you were there and where you commanded your brigade, and you explained what your area of responsibility was, what happened in Kosovo and Metohija in 1999 and before that in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Especially taking into account 1998 and 1999, particularly in 1998, there was an escalation of terrorist activity. Although terrorism is a specific phenomenon, that is to say terror that reigned in Kosovo and Metohija over centuries, 1998 was particularly characteristic because the number of attacks against civilians, members of the Ministry of the Interior and the military, escalated, and by the 30th of November, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you reading from a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a little notebook of mine, just there in order to aid my memory in terms of dates, whatever, but if you wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When did you make those notes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: He said in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Over the past ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. If it aids you, you may use the notes that you made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Though it may not arise, presumably on the basis that they will be available for inspection by us if we wish to have a look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If they are not personal notes, I see no reason why they shouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Of course. There is no problem whatsoever. In 1997, as far as I can remember there were 70 terrorist attacks over the entire year. Until the 30th of November 1998, there were about 1.470 attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you indicated just now that there was a sharp rise in terrorism in 1998, an escalation of terrorism. You were there. Why did this escalation of terrorism occur in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: In 1998, if we were to look at the individual months of 1998, in January and February, in view of the situation as it was in Kosovo and Metohija, were the usual thing. There were a few attacks then. However, from the month of March onwards, there was a particularly large number of attacks against civilians, a large number of attacks against members of the MUP. As for the army of Yugoslavia, the attacks on the army of Yugoslavia were launched only at the state border during those first few months. As for attacks on the military, they did not happen at that time. That is to say, barracks were not attacked, and the army was in-depth as far as the territory is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, who carried out these attacks already in the late 1990s?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Although terrorist groups have been present in Kosovo and Metohija with different ideologies but always with the same objective in mind since the Second World War, in the 1990s an organisation appeared. We call it the KLA, although the first part of its name doesn't sound right. "Ushtria Clirimtare e Kosoves" is its name in Albanian, or, rather, the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You didn't answer the question asked by Mr. Milosevic. Why was there an escalation of terrorism in 1998. Are you able to say why there was an escalation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain, however, that will require some more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would have to go back to 1995, to the Dayton agreement. The Albanian delegation expected that they would be invited to Dayton, to the United States of America, and that at these talks the Albanian issue would be raised as well. However, that did not happen. Although the Albanian delegation was present, they were told that in Dayton it is only the problems of peoples who were in conflict in Bosnia were being dealt with. They were not in a conflict, and practically there was no place for them in those talks. I think that a diplomat from the State Department who said that, if I remember correctly, his name was Robert Perrina. In a way, this was a green light for a crisis to start in Kosovo. So from 1995 onwards, there has been a sharp rise in the number of terrorist attacks. In 1997, I already mentioned how many there were, only about 70, whereas in 1998 there were 1.470. Quite simply, they wished to force the international community to deal with that purported problem of Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in the briefest possible terms, can you tell us what you know about this organisation you mentioned, the UCK.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: The UCK, or the KLA, is a terrorist group with a very strange ideology. Even certain international officials spoke about that. Its ideology was created by an illegal movement from the beginning of the 1980s, that is to say from 1982 onwards. To be more specific, that was called the People's Movement of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on, the witness's evidence is coming to the borders of expertise. No report's been served, of course. But for these last few observations, which are clearly not sort of nuts and bolts matters of fact with which the Chamber may be more concerned so far as this witness is concerned, it might be helpful to know on what he's relying for these expressions of clear opinion. I'm not anxious to put -- or have the Court put particularly strict parameters around evidence of a witness like this, but nevertheless as we are going to hear evidence, or if we're going to hear evidence of this kind, it would be helpful to know what his sources are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For my own part I don't find it to be -- the witness of an expert nature, and I wouldn't stop the evidence on that basis. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This terrorist group, as I've Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already said, had a strange ideology. It can be said that it moved in two directions, basically. It's a fascist Stalinist ideology, because part of that group was made up of the remains and the heirs of the fascist ideology from the Second World War. The persons who belonged to the SS division of Skenderbeg, to the Balists, that was that group. The other group were the hard-core Stalinists, supported as far back as the days of Enver Hoxha, and then Sali Berisha continued to support them. That was that group. That was the ideology of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the KLA have any political party or movement backing it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: The KLA did not have a political party. This movement or, as they called it, the Popular Movement of Kosovo, the MPK, was created by persons who, after attempting to topple the constitutional order in 1981, fled to Switzerland and Germany. They created this movement of Kosovo, the Popular Movement of Kosovo. Balli Kombitar is the fascist organisation that it basically belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in Kosovo and Metohija, apart from the KLA, was there any other terrorist organisation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: There were several terrorist groups in Kosovo. However, there was an organisation that was called FARK, in Albanian it is called Forcat e Armatosura e Republikes se Kosoves. This armed formation first appeared in June 1998 in Kosovo. It spent about three months in Kosovo, and it reappeared in 1999. This armed formation belongs to this illegal government of the Republic of Kosovo that was headed by Bujar Bukoshi. These units were established by the minister of defence in this illegal government, Ahmet Krasniqi, who was killed, I think, in Albania on the 23rd of September, 1998

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, what was the difference between the UCK and FARK? What were their goals?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: As far as goals are concerned, their goals were the same, identical; that is to say, bringing down the constitutional order of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and separating the territory of Kosovo and Metohija from it. However, their approach was different at different times. The KLA only espoused brutal force, and they used it even against their fellow countrymen who thought different, and Serbs and other Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija. On the other hand, FARK, Rugova's FARK, that is to say Rugova on the one hand, advocated a peaceful settlement of the Kosovo problem over the longer term, and on the other hand through his illegal Ministry of Defence from the 1990s he advocated military organisation and also preparation for an armed uprising in Kosovo. May I just say one more thing? In 1993, the first minister of defence in that illegal government of Kosovo, Hajzer Hajzeraj, together with like-minded individuals, conceived the first plan for an armed uprising in Kosovo and Metohija. This plan involved gathering weapons in Albania and establishing 100 platoons and 200 companies in Kosovo and Metohija, establishing several brigades that would be grouped in two corps; that is to say, the Metohija Corps and the Kosovo Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, based on their activities, their conduct, was that a terrorist organisation or could you qualify it in some other terms?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Beyond doubt the Liberation Army of Kosovo was considered, and using all parameters can be considered as a terrorist organisation. As I've already told you, its very rapid spread and expansion in Kosovo was a result of the use of brutal force or, as we call it, "the Kalashnikov strategy." This organisation was called a terrorist organisation by certain international officials as well. I think that Mr. Gelbard, an envoy of the US State Department for the Balkans, in February, if I remember it correctly, on the 22nd of February, 1998, in Pristina, said that the KLA was undoubtedly a terrorist organisation and that the United States strongly condemned terrorist activities of this organisation. He stated this in a meeting with the Albanian representatives. I know for a fact that Ibrahim Rugova was there, as were some other prominent Albanian leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, your experience from this period of time in 1998 and 1999 when it comes to armed activities of this organisation, did it only entail conflict with terrorism or anything else?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Based on everything that was happening on the ground, based on everything that I experienced personally since I was born in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and I know the mentality of the Albanian people well, so judging on all of that, I can say that this was a conflict with terrorism and terror.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In briefest possible terms, tell us, what were they waging struggle for?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: In briefest, terms, if I were to give the briefest possible answer, then I would tell you that they wanted to detach the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and annex it to the territory of the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, you brought with you the videotape which was recorded at the oath-taking ceremony in the vicinity of Djakovica in July of 1998. Could we see the footage, please, and would you please identify the persons seen on the tape. This can be seen in tab 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't show it yet.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let the video be played.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the oath-taking ceremony of the KLA in the vicinity of Junik in Djakovica municipality. The man reading out the text of the oath is Hajdin Abazi, nicknamed Lum Haxhiu. He's a teacher by profession, born in the vicinity of Gnjilane. In 1998, he was in Junik serving as a kind of a spokesperson of the units in the Dukagjin operative area. Members are taking an oath stating that they would fight until the last drop of blood or, rather, until they are united with the Republic of Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In 1998, what I wanted us to see is what concerns their goal, which is unification with the Republic of Albania, and we could see that in this footage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let us please look at the next video footage, which is also the oath-taking ceremony of those who have the same goal, showing the same person. Would you please play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the same month, June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Late May or early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the same person?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. We can see Hajdin Abazi here. He was widely known there as Lum Haxhiu. Here he is with Mr. Holbrooke in Junik. The man carrying shoes here is called Sefedin Kuci, former JNA officer. This is Lum Haxhiu.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: We can see some leaders here. Veton Surroi was on the footage. He was -- he attended the meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So in 1998 they pledged in their oath to unite with Albania. This was just several months after Mr. Gelbard claiming -- claimed that they were a terrorist organisation. And we could see a representative of the US administration with that same person advocating unification with Albania. They were together in Junik. Now let us see something relating to the bringing in of weapons, and let us see who the veterans of the KLA are.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please play the following tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this person comes from the Krasniqi family. He is an Albanian. This is a typical manner in which weapons arrived in Kosovo. This is also the area of Junik. We can see Mr. Clark here. We can see Mr. Holbrooke here. Mr. Clark here was referred to as the KLA veteran, whereas Mr. Holbrooke was called "Golden Kalashnikov."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that last clip was clearly an amalgam of different events, I think, unless it was itself was a film or documentary, I don't know what it was. It might help if we know what its number is so we can find out what we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, was that one continuous clip or was it a collection of different events? Or can the general say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can say. If you wish, I can answer. This is one film and only certain segments have been abbreviated, cut, because the entire film runs for longer than an hour. In Belgrade, I saw this film at the Commission for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. Since Mr. Tomanovic, the attorney-at-law, put in a request to be provided this film, he was the one who made this abbreviated version. This film was also shown on several TV stations in my country. I believe it was also broadcast here in the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We saw the last clip and saw that it had Dutch subtitles. You were able to see that there are several clips. One refers to the oath-taking ceremony and unification with Albania in June of 1998, and then in the next clip we saw how those people met and talked with Mr. Holbrooke in July of 1998. And then in 1999, we saw them greeting Mr. Clark as the KLA veteran and referring to Mr. Holbrooke as the "Golden Kalashnikov." So this describes the political background of the events which later on Clinton's administration tried to depict as a reaction to some humanitarian catastrophe, and there was none of that in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Evidence coming from the accused; wrong place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able -- Mr. Delic, are you able to put a date on the last segment of the film?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the date, it probably exists on the tape. I don't remember the date, but I know that this was the donors' conference during the elections in the States, the donors' dinner during the last elections in the States, in honour of Mr. Kerry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In honour of whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: John Kerry. So that means it was in the year 2004.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was a fund raising dinner in honour of Mr. Kerry. It is obvious here that this person whom we can see on the screen right now made footage in 1998 and 1999 about these visits to Kosovo. Also, the meetings with Albanian diaspora in the United States was filmed as well, and then the last segment comes from this fund raising dinner. So I understood this to be a film that this person filmed about himself and about the activities of Albanian immigrants in America.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, in order not to visit a very distant past, in view of the fact that the struggle against terrorism has been going on for many years, I would like us to focus on 1998. Would you please describe the document entitled "Excerpt from the annual intelligence report on electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic operations" for 1998, which can be found in tab 4. Would you please first tell us how you obtained this document, and is it a reliable, proper document?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. I found that. So this is the excerpt from the annual intelligence report on electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic operations for 1998. This excerpt, or this annual report was compiled by the 52nd Company for electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic operations within the Pristina Corps. This is a perfectly valid document. This is the company who performed these tasks for the purposes of the Pristina Corps. Some of the members of this company were located in my barracks in Prizren and also in another barracks in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So this is an excerpt from the annual report on electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic operations for 1998.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look, General, as I asked you to explain, please take a look at several segments which I underlined in this report. We excerpted just several pages here. On page 30 that is here as the first page, it says: "On the 13th of May, following two or three days of inactivity, the terrorists' radio communications suddenly increased in intensity as did terrorist actions." Would you please be so kind and read it yourself.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that. On the 13th of May, it says: "Following two or three days of inactivity, the terrorists' radio communications suddenly increased in intensity as did terrorist actions. There was a period of inactivity during the visit of the American representative Richard Gelbard following which the number of the attacks against the members of the RS MUP increased in several places in Kosovo and Metohija, on the Pristina-Pec and Pristina-Djakovica roads. We discovered a new frequency - 154.570 megahertz."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the 14th? Please read out just the bits that you believe to be most important in this document.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, bear in mind that you have to read slowly to allow the interpreters to keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of May, and it says here specifically from 2240 hours to 2315 hours, there was intensive conversation between two speakers. They were Guri-3 and Ekoj, the speakers. From this piece of information -- or, rather, from this conversation we are able to conclude the following: That one of these units should prepare for an attack on a police patrol and that that should take place somewhere in the Drenica region but that on the following day in the evening they would receive an exact message and that someone should go to the railway station for destruction, it says. After the attack -- after the fighting, rather, the group should take care and look after itself, not to enter into any difficult situations. So that was the conversation. Guri-3 is one of the participants in the conversation. In Serbian, "guri" means "stone."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I meant Albanian. Slip of the tongue. And the Serbian translation of "Guri" is stone, and he was one of the very active participants in this radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then this goes on to the 14th of May where it says that the terrorists, after the attack, were surrounded by strong forces.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A group of terrorists from -- what does this P/Z mean? Kodra, what that's that? It's the call-sign Kodra?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I even remember the attack. It was in my area on the 14th of May, and it was one of the attacks on the police patrol in a place called Zrze. At the crossroads of the Prizren-Djakovica roads and the local road running towards the village of Ratkovac. And you can see here that the terrorists say they were surrounded by strong MUP forces and that they are seeking reinforcements and assistance in the form of men and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now take a look at the following page. What is happening on the 10th of June? A bus is mentioned that was expected. They were expecting a bus, it says.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is about a bus which was supposed to bring in the money they had gathered for the purchase of weapons, ammunition, and other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now look at a few paragraphs further on. On the 17th of June, what does it say there? There's mention of some consultation at the headquarters in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, the village of Dobri Dol is mentioned, north of Iglarevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, General, did you have any information and intelligence about the existence of any kind of headquarters in Drenica in that village of Dobri Dol?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: The intelligence we received electronically through the radio matrix spoke about the fact that one of those staffs or headquarters of a high level was in Drenica and that one was in the surrounding area of Djakovica. Later on it was the Dukagjin Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what does the 21st of June speak about, about an expected attack on a police checkpoint at Rudnik?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The village of Rudnik, that means along the road from Pec to Mitrovica. And there was a police checkpoint there, and on several occasions the checkpoint was attacked. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Here it says that there was grouping taking place in the Mamusa village - that's my area - where there was to be a meeting of the KLA leaders. That seems to be a little strange. Well, strange. Actually, Mamusa is inhabited -- 80 per cent of Mamusa inhabitants are Turks, a Turkish population. They are the autochthonous Turks, as we call them. And most of them are in the Prizren municipality and they are only to be found in this village of Mamusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us why this is strange, why this appears change to you, whether because the Turks were not members of the KLA or for some other reason.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: We have no cases of any Turk being a member of the KLA. But as I say, the place was chosen because nobody would expect a meeting to be held at a place like that, and they felt they were safe, they'd be safe if they were to hold the meeting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now take a look at the next page, 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, bear in mind that we already have a lot of evidence from your witnesses on the KLA as an organisation, its origins and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am bearing that in mind, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, please, would you move on, let's do this as quickly as we can, and just indicate the most characteristic points so that I don't have to quote from the passages. But I have jotted them down for myself, but I'm sure you will select your own.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of page 33, the 28th of June, something that happened in Prizren linked to my own barracks there. This participant whose name was Korizi, around my barracks constantly from 1997 right up until the end of the war, they monitored the movement of the army, and every vehicle leaving the barracks compound, reports would be sent, and on that day goniometrics showed us that on the 28th of June right near the barracks at a warehouse for construction material this person Korizi was to be found. We called the police and attempted to find him. There were some unfinished houses that were being built in that area, under construction. And as you can see here, it says there was an unsuccessful search conducted by our security organs because he managed to take refuge in some bunker and weren't able to find him. Now, following on from that report, we can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you intend to go on at some length, I think we should take the break now. It's past the time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just on the other matter again of relevance, Witness K32, who testified 17th, 22nd of July, 2002, had important evidence on the activities of the 549th and evidence concerning this witness, specific evidence concerning this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just bear in mind the point where we ended so we can take it up when we return. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one matter, nothing to do with this witness who can indeed withdraw, to do with something that ought to be covered in private session, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please, but nothing to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, before I continue with the examination-in-chief, may I give you a piece of information, and this is it: I have checked out with Mr. Tomanovic what Mr. Nice mentioned, that on some documents they're dated 2002. Those are dates which signify the time when the copy was made and confirm that the copy is an authentic representation of the original within the same institution, that is to say the general staff of the army of Yugoslavia. My associates, with respect to the activities of the units that were under the command of General Delic, received at the end of last year, that is to say 2004, at the end, over 10.400 documents which they had to look through, and then of those 10.400 documents, which of course it was impossible to present here along with the testimony of a witness, they reduced that number to 620-odd documents. So that that was the time needed to do that, and I should like you to bear that in mind. Of course, that includes over a hundred videotapes, and they selected just 20 of those, about 20. A great selection had to be made because only six per cent of those documents were selected to be presented here of the 10.400 documents that were in existence, as I said. And as far as Mr. Nice said, that there were some A markings along with the number, there was an A, A always refers to the English translation, so it is not a new document. If the number is, say, 333 of the original document, then 333 A would be the English version, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what you just said you can include in the document which you must present tomorrow by way of explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, on page 33 of the report we were dealing with, at the bottom, towards the bottom of the page there is a date there, 21st of July 1998, and it says that they continually monitored the movement of our forces and kept checking the situation at the positions they had seized. Who is the "they"? Who monitored whom? Tell us a little about that in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, all movements of the armed forces and the police, whether from their barracks or along the roads, the communication lines, were monitored from set positions, and reports were sent out to the KLA headquarters and other KLA positions in-depth, in the rear, about the movements of every column and even every individual military or police vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now on page 41, paragraph 5, the date there is the 25th of April 1998, there is a dialogue between somebody there. Now, who is this speaking and what is that all about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Page 41, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the date again?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 25th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here quite obviously we're dealing with a conversation between two KLA members, and the first says: "Many Serbs are moving out of this area here." And the second person says: "Just let them go. We don't need them here, this is ours." Then the first person: "Yes, if we keep on frightening them like this, no one will stay." Number 2: "Many army and police members' families have moved out of Djakovica recently. When the other Serbs find out about that, they're going to leave too." Number 1, the first speaker: "Don't talk about anything on the phone, because the Serbs can hear it. They can get the information. Tell Ruzda to say nothing over the phone. Did you get the money?" And then the line breaks off there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 42, paragraph 7, we have the 8th of June, 1998, as the date, and we have somebody's words saying: "We were told here in Switzerland that everybody from 18 to 55 to put on --" "We were told here in Switzerland that an order was issued for everyone between 18 and 55 to put on a KLA uniform." Who is this speaking? What's this about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Another participant in a conversation monitored, calling up from Switzerland, calling one of his relatives, and he's asking whether that piece of information is correct, that the KLA is mobilising one and all and making lists for all the individuals in Kosovo and Metohija, especially in the villages, of individuals ranging between the ages of 18 and 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A little in front of that the date is the 11th of May, and it says: "The KLA is everywhere, some of us are here, too. We'll get there from Germany in no time. We hear the vicinity of Decani is full of our people. Be careful about what you do, we don't want to die for nothing." What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: That is also a conversation. One person was from Metohija and the other person was in Germany, and they were having a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on that same page --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The interesting problematic area here: The witness doesn't produce this material himself. It seems we're now firmly in the area of some kind of intercepted material. We didn't produce material, I think, in this way. We produced intercepts properly sourced and evidenced with reports in advance. Not foreshadowed by the 65 ter summary, no report. How am I going to deal with it? Is this confidential or secret material of a kind that's going to be available to me, or are we going to get this report and nothing more? Another example of the real difficulty of this accused determinedly not serving material like this in advance with reports, not using the provisions of 89(F), and leaving the Prosecution in a very restricted position so far as assisting the Trial Chamber by cross-examination in due course is concerned. The Chamber may decide it's outside the area for which this witness is most likely to be helpful; that's a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, the witness has indicated the origins of this document, and he said that it was a unit which dealt with electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic equipment and said that part of that unit was located within the frameworks of his own unit. He indicated the source of the material, so we're dealing with information and intelligence that a specialised military unit came by by listening in to the radio communication going on among the KLA terrorist organisation, and the witness explained all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What isn't clear to me, Mr. Milosevic and the witness, is what puts this witness in a position to offer an interpretation as to these passages in the intercepts?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Mr. Robinson, you notice that the witness very often says, "This happened in my vicinity," or "in the vicinity of our barracks," or words to that effect, or "we called up the police to find the perpetrators," the individuals, and the police were unsuccessful in their searches, and so forth. But I'm going to ask the witness now to give us any additional information if he feels it necessary how he comes to be in a position to be able to provide us with explanations with respect to this report and these excerpts about electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you add anything to that, General?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: This is an annual intelligence report, and annual intelligence reports are compiled at the end of a year, calendar year. However, they would not have any value as far as I was concerned as a piece of information and intelligence had I just received them at the end of the year. What happened was this was on a daily basis. Whenever necessary, from one minute to the next, from one hour to the next, I would receive information and intelligence coming in which was of vital importance to me about the units or parts of units. One was in the barracks in Prizren and the other in my barracks in Djakovica. And the information provided was even more detailed. Of course, we weren't able to include all the pieces of information and intelligence in the annual report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you explain, Mr. Delic, why the dates jump about in the -- they're not all in sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just once. If you could take a look at page 38 in B/C/S, Mr. Delic. The bottom of the page ends up with the report dated 13th of December. You follow? And we are -- and we are missing page 40, and then from page 41 it begins with 20th of April. Is this a document which is contiguous? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. This report contains many more pages, and it also involves many different areas. One of the areas are the intercepts of conversations between terrorists. What you see here is not really followed by the dates. I have the opportunity of seeing the entire report. These are dates that have to do with terrorism. But probably because the legal advisors asked for this unit to provide something which would be of interest and which pertained to my area of responsibility primarily, that is probably why they selected these particular pages. And that is why there are these interruptions, in a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that doesn't deal with the question that's being asked. It goes to December and then we're back in April on subsequent pages. Now, what's the explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given this is an annual report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My only explanation of this could be is that this report follows dozens of different areas, and that is why there can be this kind of page difference, because there were excerpts from different areas that pertain to my zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's now -- it's now, in my submission, quite clear this evidence shouldn't be allowed in. In the Prosecution's case with intercepts, there was a careful and meticulous presentation with either evidence of who had listened to the intercept and a setting out of the circumstances, or the intercept itself available. Here we've got some selection of material, apparently made by the accused's associates. The witness himself hasn't made the selection, so he's in no position to say whether it's representative or not. We haven't got any of the intercepts themselves. We haven't got anybody who says they listened to them and wrote them down. How can it be of any value to you? In the circumstances, where there are apparently 600 exhibits and where this witness may have matters of detail on issues in the indictment to deal with, can we not move on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, does this go to admissibility?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kay, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the Prosecution case when we had issues of admissibility of the intercepts, the Prosecution initially presented that evidence in the forms of just transcripts and eventually, because the evidence concerned the acts and conduct of the accused, were forced to bring evidence that was more proximate to the production of the materials into evidence, and the Trial Chamber will remember the particular witness who gave evidence about those intercepts. In this case here we're not concerned with evidence that is relevant to the acts and conduct of the accused, more peripheral evidence dealing with the background to issues within the case, which seems to arise from this report that was produced in 1998 demonstrating the existence of this kind of material and what it displayed in terms of background at that time to events that were happening within Kosovo. In our submission, for the limited purposes that this evidence goes towards the indictment, it is relevant evidence as far as it goes to the case, and in those circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the limited purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the background to the indictment, the strength of the KLA, the KLA activities, and the policy of the KLA which arises within this report. And for those purposes, this witness is giving evidence about these materials which apparently were in the possession of the VJ at that time in 1998 and the issues that they were aware that the KLA were involved in conducting. And in that regard, the state of mind of the commanders of VJ brigades, such as this particular witness or other witnesses, is obviously relevant to issues concerning the state of mind of the accused in 1998, which is when I take --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice says that the witness himself didn't listen to the intercepts. He didn't write the -- down -- he didn't write down the passages, the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He wouldn't have, and no one expects a general to have been involved in that particular form of event. What he is, he's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. producing materials that go to the state of mind, if you like, of the general and other -- other members of the VJ, and by that the state of mind that is relevant for this accused in relation to issues within this indictment. This is part of the materials that was in existence at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to remind the Chamber, it's not a question of the Prosecution being forced to do something. What happened was that intercepts were produced to witnesses who, as with all intercepts, listened to the intercept in their entirety. The witness was either able to say something about who the people speaking were or sometimes about the context, or both. The intercepts were then marked for identification, and the Chamber's standard was that it was required that we produce a witness or the witness who could deal with the provenance and the technicalities and mechanics of provenance of the documents otherwise marked for identification. That's the standard that the Chamber set, and there's no reason why it should be any different. They didn't all concern the acts and conducts of the accused specifically; they contained a wide range of matters, including his own acts and conduct. Second thing is, this is clearly a selection. We don't know the criteria upon which the selection has been made, and I'm not going to be able to ask the associates about it, and I'm not going to be able to ask this witness about it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber was minded to require that a better foundation be laid for the admission of this evidence, but bearing in mind that the witness has given evidence that he read these transcripts, we believe that a sufficient foundation has been laid, and we'll hear the evidence accordingly. But, Mr. Milosevic, bear in mind that we already have evidence on the background leading up to the conflict. This is repetitive. If you must deal with it, then deal with it as briefly as possible and let's move on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try to save time, Mr. Robinson, but you saw from what the witness said at the very beginning that he commanded units that covered a very big part of the territory, and many of the accusations levelled have to do with things that happened precisely in that part of the territory. So we have to see what the military knew and what the military did in that part of the territory where Mr. Nice claims certain things happened the way he formulated it and the way he saw it. As for this remark made by Mr. Kwon or, rather, this observation made by Mr. Kwon, there is no doubt that it wasn't my associates who made these cuts in these reports. In the first part, it has to do with specific events, and it goes all the way to the end of December. And then on page 41, there are communications between them and there are direct quotations. Then again, in terms of dates, again they go back to 1998. As for Mr. Nice's remark that he always tried to explain who and how obtained these intercepts, I hope that the witness explained very clearly that this was done by a special unit of the army of Yugoslavia through electronic surveillance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I did not call on you to speak. I had ruled in your favour. If I am going to rule in your favour having heard Mr. Nice and Mr. Kay, I don't call on you, so you don't need to address the issue any more. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on page 42, General, in this paragraph that has to do with the 8th of June, the one that you already quoted, when Switzerland was mentioned. At the beginning of the paragraph it says: "The electricity poles that were knocked down - if anyone asks, tell them the Serbs did it." And then 2 is probably the other interlocutor: "You have a rifle, you don't care if you get killed." 1: "We were told that within two weeks a decision will be made for international troops to enter Kosovo. We were told here in Germany that all of us must voluntarily donate 1.000 Deutschmarks respectively for Kosovo." What does that show? He mentions what was said to them. He's speaking from Germany, and he's saying that they were told that international forces are to enter Kosovo. What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: In this first part, Mr. Milosevic, since at the beginning of the year a considerable part of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija came under terrorist control, the main transmission lines were broken down between Kosovo and Metohija. That's probably the reference that was made. And in this second part, this is a well-known fact: In Germany, Switzerland, and other Western European countries, it was already Bukoshi's illegal government that imposed a tax, and until 1998 it was 3 per cent of all the income of all Albanians, and later it was raised to 5 per cent. In addition to that, the KLA levied its own tax depending on the income of each and every Albanian, and this fund was called The Homeland Is Calling. Those were the contributions that were used for buying weapons later on in Albania and other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, and what is mentioned here, that they were told that within two weeks' time a decision would be made for international forces to enter Kosovo. Did that have anything to do with the intensification of their activity?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Certainly. I saw in several sections of these reports that people, Albanians in Western European countries, are telling those that are in Kosovo and Metohija that they should persevere for another week or two and that there would certainly be an intervention by international forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. On page 49, the date is the 26th of September, 1998. It says: "From unofficial Siptar sources we found out that there are currently more than 5.000 members of the KLA." Whose knowledge is this?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: This is already the month of September. This comes from several intercepts. That is how this fact was arrived at. If I'm allowed to say a few things here that are very important. Our estimates showed that in the month of September, after the anti-terrorist drive carried out by the army of Yugoslavia and the forces of the Ministry of the Interior, those anti-terrorist actions were in accordance with a particular plan and they went on for two months. The number of terrorists was 25 to 30.000 in the month of June and July, and it was brought down to only 5.000 then. Many of them threw their weapons away, and a number crossed over to Albania. So in the month of September in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, according to our estimates, there were about 5.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General, how do you know the source of this information as to the number of KLA in the several intercepts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that this is an annual report and that it was made on the basis of daily reports. So probably on the basis of several pieces of information that showed that the number of members of the KLA in that period was brought down to about 5.000. As for our own information, through our security service we had information daily about the KLA. And independently from this, our estimate was that after the anti-terrorist drive in Kosovo, there were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is not the number of KLA but the source of information. This passage specifically refers to the unofficial Siptar sources, but you referred to several intercepts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was how do you remember that this was based on several intercepts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here from unofficial Siptar sources. That is to say intercepts, intercepts of conversations taking place between Siptars at home and abroad when they were discussing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, on page 50, the 28th of September reads that Siptars were advised, if they were running away, to go in groups of 1.000 or 2.000. What kind of information is this and how was that obtained?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: This information also came from intercepts, from radio contacts between the KLA members and their channels that were surveilled by the 52nd Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Under the 3rd of October on that same page, it is stated that: "Information was released that NATO had completed its operations for using technical equipment for firing on Serbian targets in Serbia." Please tell us, what did the reports for that date, the 3rd of October, state?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: This refers to the information to the effect that NATO had completed its preparations for firing on Serbian targets. Then it also mentions the number of planes that had already been prepared to that end and then what members of NATO provided planes for such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And before that, on the 1st of October, it reads: "Siptars who used to be KLA members continue to leave the territory of the FRY, mostly to Albania, but there are cases of some of them moving to Hungary" through certain channels. Is that something that you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: After the anti-terrorist drive that was completed on the 28th of September, 1998, part of the Siptar population and the vast majority of the KLA members left the territory of Kosovo and Metohija as did all members of FARK, which were organised in three -- which had been organised in three brigades and were located in the Dukagjin area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, under the 4th of October it says that the KLA soldiers were trained in Tirana, Kukes, Korca, Gjirokastra, Durres, and Oruga. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Our information, the information that we had within the army of Yugoslavia dating back to 1991 indicated in what locations members of the KLA and members of terrorist groups were trained in Albania. So this information listed here under the 4th of October is -- was nothing new. It simply confirmed the information that we had previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 51, the date of 17th of October is listed, and it says here that a conversation which took place between a Siptar from the Netherlands and a Siptar from Kosovo and Metohija was intercepted. What is this about? What are they discussing here?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: It simply confirms what I stated previously; namely, that one of them who was a member of the KLA and the other person, who was in the Netherlands, the first one said that almost half of the KLA members from Kosovo and Metohija were in Albania and then says that the majority of their leaders, and then under quotation marks "were loaded 'with money.'" And then further on for the 17th of October, it is stated that based on the agreement signed in Belgrade in October, NATO planes, reconnaissance planes, started flying over Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the same page, under the 22nd of October, it reads that Solana reached an agreement with Macedonian Prime Minister on the possible use of NATO bases for operations on the territory of Kosovo. What does this report contain and how did you obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: This was obtained in the same manner. I think that this is a widely known fact, a fact that was known to the public in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, on page 22, under the 2nd November of 1998 -- on page 52, it is stated that all Serbs who have remained in villages should be driven out and that they will take revenge against anyone who fought against them, including Siptars who did not want to take part in conflict. And then they warn their relatives abroad not to come this winter because war would break out again in the spring. Who stated this and what does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: Once again, this deals with the members of the KLA, starting in March. The Serbian residents living in over 80 villages where they constituted minority left their properties and moved into towns. So this here refers to the Serbs who remained in villages, and at least in my area of responsibility very few such Serbs remained. And according to this they had to be driven out as well. And that Siptars who did not want to take part in combat, because there were such individuals and such villages, and those who refused to return weapons in September and October, that they would face drastic consequences and measures, which is exactly what happened later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you were asked is who said this. What's the source of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source is the same; intercepted conversations between Siptars who were members of the liberation army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps you'll excuse me for saying it doesn't look at all like that. It's not in quotations, which most of the intercepts are. It's a reference to "they" rather than an individual, and it's talking about warning their cousins abroad. Do you really know where that came from? It also, by the way, follows a reference to press comments on the previous page in relation to the 30th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, my request in relation to this particular item was, in light of the witness's answer, was to the effect, can I please be provided by the accused with the intercepts, and all of them, on which this document is based. It will take some time for me to review them, but I'll try and find the resources, and then I'll review them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The intercepts must be provided to the Prosecutor. Are they available?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing but this report. I asked the general when the report was compiled, and he said that this was the report for 1998 drafted by this reconnaissance unit, and the unit could have only drafted this based on the information it gathered in the course of listening in on the radio communications. So this was compiled in late 1998, and it concerns their activity for 1998. This is the unit that regularly does this type of work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying they're not available? Because all of this will go to the weight that the Chamber will attach.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not saying so. Perhaps they are available. I don't have access to archives of such units. I didn't even have these documents until my associates obtained them. But undoubtedly this is a document that was compiled at the time based on the information collected by that unit. They must have had thousands and thousands of pieces of information flowing to them, and they included in their report what they believed to be most important for their report for 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what you say, but there's no evidence at the moment of when this was compiled.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was stated by the witness that this report was compiled for 1998. I heard him say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For 1998. What we don't have is evidence of when it was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: General, can you assist, please? Can you give us explanations concerning this material?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR DELIC
utterances.text: This activity, electronic reconnaissance and anti-electronic operations, is an activity that goes round the clock, 24 hours a day. The information is provided instantaneously to everybody who might be interested in the information and to whom the information pertains, because otherwise they would be valueless and would not be subject to use unless they were provided instantaneously. The annual report compiles or uses the bits that were typical or were important. Everything else, the other bits of communication between the participants, if it was unimportant, did not enter the annual report because the objective of this report is to conduct an analysis of work, an analysis of developments in the electronic field, analysis of new frequencies used by terrorist forces, and if possible, to conduct identification of participants, meaning the commanders of the KLA units, their staffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you're being asked is when was the report - the report - compiled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have reviewed the entire annual report, I can tell you that it was compiled or drafted probably in early January 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know that. You know that it was drafted in January -- early January 1999, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the army of Yugoslavia, generally all analyses are completed at the level of the units up to the level of the brigade in January; at the level the corps, that's done in February; and at the level of the army of Yugoslavia, that's done in March. Since this is a company, that's the level of this unit, this is a company within a corps, then it is certain that this analysis was done in January based on all daily reports from 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And how available is the report once it's completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This report was sent by the company for electronic reconnaissance to the corps command, which is the superior command, and then to the communications sector and sector for informations and electronic activities within the general staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It must be classified in some way, is it? What classification does it have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that this was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. classified as strictly confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No higher than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, certainly not higher than that. Above that there is only the state level classification, and this document does not warrant that type of classification, the state secret classification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even though it discloses the extent to which you were able to listen in to the activities of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said in how many copies this report was done. Since my last post before retiring was acting chief of the operations administration, which is the administration making or drafting all orders for the army command. Therefore, I know very clearly what warrants state secret classification or strictly confidential classification or internal document. This falls in the strictly confidential category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have the complete document with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this document in Belgrade in 2002, but I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour forecast perhaps what I would be asking is that I would like to be provided with a full copy of the report up to pages 33 and then the missing pages 30 -- whatever we've got missing, 32 and 33, I think, is it, 34 and 35, and then 39 and 40, and everything else. There's obviously now no -- on the witness's explanation, there is no grounds why we shouldn't receive or be allowed to see all of the report along with the original intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, are the original intercepts available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the original intercepts, that could be verified through the general staff. I'm not informed about this, but as for the material, I think we can obtain all the missing pages. However, there is a part of the report which most likely the general staff would not provide, and I can tell you in private session the reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's -- we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's suggesting the missing pages, the incompleteness of the document, suggests that it is entirely unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The issue of the missing pages is perhaps capable of explanation by the Defence, and the general has attempted to explain that. His assertions as to unreliability are just general assertions he's making against the Defence using this document. The general has tried to deal with that and has given an explanation. He's established that it's probative and relevant to the extent that the material in 1998 is relevant to the trial, but the issue of unreliability is just being asserted by Mr. Nice without any foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll just respond to that in this way: First of all, I'm going to carry on asking for material that's necessary to allow for the possible timely cross-examination of a witness, but if a responsible advocate appearing for this accused wanted to turn up with part of a document of which the other part was going to be subject to protection or with being withheld by a party, he would make that -- make that position clear to the Chamber straight away. If he was going to produce a document based on intercepts, knowing that the intercepts weren't available to him, he would make that clear to the Chamber straight away so that the Chamber could know from the beginning what were the limitations on the document and its potential shortcomings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Remember Mr. Milosevic is not a professional advocate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I understand that, and it's with that in mind that I've been slow to object to this document and wait and see what was going to emerge from the questions and answers of the non-professional advocate and his witness, but that's actually the standard that we ought to have in mind, and it's with that in mind that when we reach this position, I make the requirements and requests that I do. They either serve as quite legitimate requests to have underlying material that one would expect to be provided or they serve to show that the material is in its present form simply unreliable. The timing of my request, I could, of course, simply wait in a process that's going to clearly be extended with this witness, until the moment when I ask him questions, I then say to him, Can I have the intercepts? He says, Yes, they are available but it will take a week to get them. Too late. Far better that I make the request now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is the Limaj case here? A Status Conference. Fifteen past two. We'll have to adjourn now, Mr. Milosevic, and I will allow you to speak first thing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. The document is authentic. The general confirmed that. The excerpts start with page 30, not because someone wants to hide the first 30 pages but because it was thought that they weren't relevant for the purposes of these proceedings, for proving anything here. So the fact that some pages are missing has nothing to do with the claims being made about challenging the authenticity of the document at all, and the witness himself has confirmed its authenticity. As for Mr. Nice's statements that I can access those documents before him, that's absolutely not true. My associates have informed me that the office of Mr. Nice received the documents having to do with 1998, having to do with the activities of the units under this witness's command more than a year before them, and this was in 2003, and I mentioned that. So if Mr. Nice needs anything and needs to access anything, he can request it from those who will provide him with it before they provide me with it, and he cannot tell me what I -- what excerpts I'm going to present here as evidence and exhibits. That's up to me. It's my affair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we're going to adjourn now. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of June, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
